activities.caption: arithmetic versus geometric — drag the divider
activities.name: seqFamCompare

config.prompt: Two families of growth — drag the divider:

before.label: arithmetic
before.text: adds a fixed amount each step — steady, linear, predictable (savings with a flat bonus)

after.label: geometric
after.text: multiplies by a fixed factor — slow at first, then unstoppable (compound interest)

config.why: Every 'exponential surprise' — in finance, epidemics, technology adoption — is this picture: the compounding curve hides below the line, then pulls away without limit.

config.prompt: The sequence 5, 8, 11, 14, … has nth term 3n + 2. Roughly what is the 100th term?
config.why: 3 × 100 + 2 = 302 — the position-to-term rule answers 'what is the 100th term?' in one line, no walking required.
config.context: the first term, plus (n − 1) steps of size d

config.root: Is 100 a term of 5, 8, 11, 14, …? Solving 3n + 2 = 100 gives n = 32⅔. What is the verdict?

choices.label: Yes — n exists, so it is a term
choices.feedback: No: n must be a whole number — 32⅔ is not a position in the sequence.

choices.label: No — n is not a whole number, so 100 is not a term
choices.feedback: Right — the nth term is also a membership test: only whole-number n count.

choices.label: Yes — round n up to 33
choices.feedback: Rounding is illegal here: term 33 is 101, not 100.

no.text: A position number cannot be two-thirds of anything.

right.text: 'Which term equals 50?' — the term-to-term rule cannot say; the nth term answers in one line.

round.text: The sequence steps 5, 8, 11, … never lands on 100.

config.why: The nth term answers 'where is any term?' directly — and membership too.

activities.caption: fill the blanks — the quadratic sequence's certificate
activities.name: seqQuadCloze

config.text: The sequence 2, 3, 6, 11, 18 has differences 1, 3, 5, 7 — a second difference constant at %%0%%. That constant second difference certifies a quadratic nth term with a equal to %%1%% the second difference.
config.hint: The gap between the gaps, and what fraction of it becomes the leading coefficient.

activities.caption: pair each classic with its story
activities.name: seqClassicMatch

config.prompt: Pair each classic sequence with its description:

pairs.right: dots stacked in triangles; nth term n(n+1)/2
each term the sum of the previous two
the limit of Fibonacci's consecutive-term ratio, 1.618…

config.why: Fibonacci models genuinely recursive processes — rabbit populations, branching plants, spiral shells.

config.prompt: 500 bacteria double every 20 minutes. Roughly how many after 2 hours?
config.why: Six doublings: 500 × 2⁶ = 32,000 — the exponent counts the steps taken, not the term number.
config.context: the same rule runs depreciation in reverse: 20,000 × 0.85ⁿ

config.prompt: One of these claims about the chessboard rice is wrong — click it:
lines: More than two thousand times the modern annual world harvest.
Each term of a doubling sequence is less than the sum of all its predecessors.
config.correction: Each term of a geometric sequence with ratio above 1 exceeds the sum of all its predecessors — the 64th square holds more than squares 1 through 63 combined.
config.why: Most of any doubling's total arrives in its final steps — the mathematical shape of the word 'suddenly'.

activities.anchor: asked as a schoolboy to add 1 through 100
activities.caption: rebuild Gauss's pairing trick
activities.name: seqGaussOrder

config.prompt: Rebuild Gauss's three moves — what comes first:
items: Add the columns — every pair sums to 101
config.why: Nothing here is special to 100: the same three lines give the general formula n(n + 1)/2 that the triangular numbers were quietly using all along.

activities.anchor: A patient takes 200 mg of a drug each day
activities.caption: call the steady state
activities.name: seqSteadyEst

config.prompt: A patient takes 200 mg of a drug daily; the body clears 60% each day (r = 0.4). Roughly what steady-state level does the amount on board approach?
config.why: a/(1 − r) = 200/0.6 ≈ 333 mg — infinitely many doses, finite accumulation, which is why dosing schedules are designed the way they are.
config.context: the first dose sometimes starts with a 'loading' amount

activities.anchor: shrink to zero yet the sum diverges
activities.caption: true or false — the harmonic trap
activities.name: seqHarmJudge

config.statement: If a series' terms tend to zero, the series must sum to something finite.
config.why: Terms tending to zero is necessary but not sufficient — the harmonic series 1 + ½ + ⅓ + … diverges, passing 10 only after about 12,000 terms.
